title: Can a sealed class or interface be local or anonymous, and why not?
shortTitle: Can a sealed class/interface be local or anonymous: why not?
keyPoints: A sealed class or interface cannot be local (declared inside a method) or anonymous.
Sealing requires an explicit, stable set of permitted subtypes identified by name in the `permits` clause.
A local class has a name scoped to one method body, so it cannot appear in a `permits` clause outside that method.
An anonymous class has no name at all, so there is nothing to list as a permitted subtype.
The compiler records permitted subtypes in the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute, which requires resolvable binary names.
A lambda also cannot implement a sealed interface, because the compiler cannot synthesize a named permitted subtype for it.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sealing needs named, compile-time-known heirs, and local and anonymous classes have no stable name to put on the permits list, so they can never be sealed.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sealed requirement** – a sealed class or interface needs an explicit, stable set of permitted subtypes identified by fully qualified names in the `permits` clause or inferred from the same source file.
- **Local class** – declared inside a method body, its name is scoped to that method and cannot be referenced from a `permits` clause outside the method.
- **Anonymous class** – has no name at all, so there is nothing to list as a permitted subtype or as the sealing type itself.
- **Class-file attribute** – the compiler records permitted subtypes in the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute using resolvable binary names, which local and anonymous classes lack.
- **Lambda exclusion** – a lambda cannot implement a sealed interface because the compiler cannot synthesize a named permitted subtype for it.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India issuing a sealed rulebook that says "only these three named account products may extend AccountProduct: Savings, Current, and FixedDeposit." For that rule to mean anything, each permitted product must have an official, registered name that auditors can look up. A local class is like a scribble a teller makes on a sticky note inside one counter session. An anonymous class is like an unnamed temporary helper with no nameplate at all. You cannot put a scribble or a nameless helper on an official permit list.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A sealed class or interface restricts which types may extend or implement it, and every permitted subtype must be a named type known at compile time, because the compiler records that closed set in the class file's `PermittedSubclasses` attribute. A local class and an anonymous class can never be sealed. A local class has a name that exists only inside one method, so it can never be referenced from a permits clause elsewhere, and an anonymous class has no name at all.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, Pankaj designs sealed interfaces like `AccountProduct` that permit exactly three named records: savings, current, and fixed deposit. That closed set matches the compliance requirement that an auditor must be able to enumerate every possible product type. Rajesh's savings account and Priya's current account both map to permitted records, and because the set is closed, an exhaustive switch computes monthly charges with no default branch.

When a junior engineer tried to introduce a promotional product as a local sealed class inside a method, the compiler rejected it, and that rejection is the feature working correctly. A lambda also cannot implement a sealed interface, for the same naming and closed-set reasons. The only way a local or anonymous class can participate in a sealed hierarchy is through a `non-sealed` branch, which reopens the hierarchy at that point.

The practical takeaway is that sealed hierarchies should always be modeled with named, top-level or nested types, using records where possible. This gives both the closed-set guarantee and clean pattern-matching support that a regulated banking system needs.

Remember one sentence: sealing requires named, compile-time-known heirs, so local classes (method-scoped names) and anonymous classes (no names) can never be sealed.
